question: The classification of soya as a raw material with a high risk of indirect land-use change (ILUC) will effectively rule out soyabean oil as a feedstock for biofuel production. Around 20 % of soyabean oil is made as a by-product in the production of soyabean meal, which is the most important source of vegetable protein for European livestock farming.

If the market for soyabean oil collapses, it will put the economic viability of domestic oilseed processing at risk, as well as being at odds with the EU’s protein strategy. Raw materials from cultivated biomass certified under the Renewable Energy Directive are already subject to strict sustainability criteria and a cap. 1.

What is the Commission’s methodological basis for the high-ILUC classification of soya, given that it is grown primarily to meet the demand for protein, and that the use of soyabean oil for energy purposes is simply maintaining the economic viability of domestic processing?

Has the Commission assessed the risks that the measure might cause the creation of value to move outside the EU and further increase dependency on soyabean meal imports, rather than boosting European security of supply?
Why is the Commission sticking to the blanket classification – which is triggering new trade conflicts, including with the US – rather than relying on precise proof of origin?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) Emissions due to indirect land-use change (ILUC) have been found to be capable of negating some or all greenhouse gas emissions savings of individual biofuels.

While the level of greenhouse gas emissions caused by ILUC cannot be unequivocally determined, the highest risks of ILUC have been identified for biofuels produced from feedstock for which a significant expansion of the production area into land with high-carbon stock is observed.

Against this background, the Renewable Energy Directive1 sets out that the share of high ILUC-risk biofuels that is counted towards the targets for renewable energy must not exceed the level of consumption of such fuels in 2019 and is gradually decreased to zero by 2030 unless they are certified to be low ILUC-risk biofuels. This applies independently of the origin of the feedstock.

The Directive requires the Commission to review the Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/807 as regards the determination of high ILUC-risk feedstock and the certification of low ILUC-risk biofuels based on the report on feedstock expansion2. In line with the legal base, high ILUC-risk feedstocks are determined at global level and certification of low ILUC-risk biofuels is based on precise proofs of origin.

The review found that the approach set out in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/807 is appropriate. The data in the updated report on feedstock expansion shows that both palm oil and soybeans qualify as high ILUC-risk feedstock. The production of by-products is taken into account under the applied methodology.
Negative impacts on European security of supply are not expected, as the cultivation of soybeans in the EU depends only to a limited extent on the biofuel outlet and global markets are liquid.
